title: How words are built
goal: Read a word you have never met by recognising the shape it was poured into.

sections.body: A Hebrew word is a root poured into a pattern — a מִשְׁקָל. The root carries the meaning, the pattern says what kind of word it is: a place, a tool, a trade, an abstraction. Learn eight patterns and a large part of the dictionary stops needing to be looked up.

sections.caption: Patterns worth knowing on sight
head: pattern
what it makes
example
rows: מִטְבָּח — kitchen, from ט־ב־ח, to cook
מַפְתֵּחַ — key, from פ־ת־ח, to open
the trade that does it all day
the person who is like that
שַׂחְקָן — actor, from שׂ־ח־ק, to play
the place that sells or holds it
an adjective made from a noun

sections.body: The value of this is not tidiness. It is that an unknown word stops being opaque: מַצְלֵמָה is the מַקְטֵלָה tool pattern over צ־ל־ם, to photograph, so it is the thing you photograph with, and you have translated camera without a dictionary.

items.en: a bakery — the ־ִיָּה place, over א־פ־ה, to bake
a thief — the קַטָּל trade, over ג־נ־ב, to steal

sections.body: This is also why a Hebrew dictionary is organised by root rather than by spelling, and why looking a word up means stripping ו, ה, ב, ל, כ, מ, שׁ off the front and the pattern off around it first.

The patterns are productive, which is how the language absorbed a century of new things without borrowing much: מַדְפֶּסֶת, printer, is the tool pattern over ד־פ־ס, and was made the same way מַפְתֵּחַ was, three thousand years earlier.
